Too Good To Go · Brand Campaign · Copywriter Case Study

This campaign gives surplus food its authors back. Not a film. A format any of our 180,000 partners can shoot... but we'll get into that.

Presenter mode · everything starts closed. Open each as you go.
00 Start here The Brief What Too Good To Go actually asked for, in plain English.

Too Good To Go wants to lean less on paid ads and grow the organic way: by winning back the pile of people who heard of it years ago, maybe tried it once, then drifted. The job is one brand campaign built on a single idea, stretched across a manifesto, billboards, an email and social, with a short rationale. It's a behavioral nudge, not a discount-and-download conversion push.

Objective

Foster organic growth and re-engagement. Ease reliance on paid UA, which loses efficiency as markets mature.

Audience

The Conscious Shopper. Urban, 25–35. Lapsed, aware non-users.

The insight

Shift surplus from "stigmatized leftovers" to amazing things waiting to be discovered.

Main message

There's an abundance of good stuff waiting with Too Good To Go. (Express it, don't repeat it.)

Tone

Witty not sarcastic. Playful not childish. Confident not arrogant. Rebellious not provocative.

What they don't want

No lower-funnel tactics. No niche-activist positioning. No charity or food-insecurity framing.

The trap

The brief says brand campaign, not conversion, then lists "registrations and first orders rise" as a goal. Weak entries sneak in promo codes and "download now." This one holds the brand line and lets the idea do the converting.

01 The platform The Idea: "Meet Your Maker" Surplus food isn't stigmatized because it's old. It's stigmatized because it's anonymous.
People don't avoid surplus food because it's bad. They avoid it because it's nobody's.

"Leftovers" is what we call food with no author. It belongs to no one, so no one misses it. But no food is actually anonymous. Someone was up before dawn making it. Give the food its maker back and the stigma has nowhere to live.

So the focus of this campaign isn't an ad. It's an episode: fifteen seconds, a face, a name, a craft, one dry line, end card. Every shop is its own hero, in its own neighborhood, in its own words.

Everything else in this deck (the billboards, the email, all of it) is that episode, re-expressed. The pun is played completely straight; the phrase brings its own dark little grin and we never once acknowledge it.

Meet Your Maker.
Authorless "leftovers" ↓ Somebody's best work. Signed.

No casting hierarchy, no hero food, no campaign clock. Every shop is its own hero episode: the footage flows to TGTG, gets our branding, and runs on our channels city by city, and the shop gets its own cut back for its own promotion (sections 05 and 06). Too Good To Go works with 180,000+ food businesses in 21 countries. Most campaigns are one idea stretched thin. This one is 180,000 introductions that haven't happened yet.

Guardrail

The maker is never a victim, they're the hero. The second this campaign asks anyone to feel sorry for a baker, it dies and becomes the charity ad the brief banned. Nobody here needs saving. The food just needs eating.

02 Deliverable 01 · Manifesto The north star 130 words, in the maker's voice.

You've been enjoying my work for years, but we've never met.

It's nice to finally put a face to a flavor.

Funny thing is, you know your barista's name, her dog's name, and exactly where she stands on oat milk.

But the baker who made your bread? The chef who rolled your sushi? The person who stocked the case before you got there?

No idea.

And whatever's left at closing?

I made that too.

Same hands. Same recipe. Same standards.

There is no second, worse version of me that clocks in at 5 p.m.

So I'm done being anonymous.

Because the trash can has never cared who made something.

I do.

Nobody here needs saving. The food just needs eating.

Pick up a bag before we close.


Meet your maker.

130 / 150 words
03 Deliverable 02a · Out-of-Home Three billboards Stills from the episodes. The maker's line is the headline.

Every board comes out of that maker's episode: their face, one of their lines as the headline, and the lockup as the constant sign-off. Because the boards are cast from the episode shoots, OOH production collapses to a media buy, and every board runs within walking distance of its own shop. Here's three from the Copenhagen network:

Why this never wears out: "Meet your maker" is the constant, but a different human says something new on every board, in every neighborhood, in every market. The campaign line can run for years because it never has to carry a board alone. 

Real, and said out loud Lagkagehuset and Meny are real, publicly documented Too Good To Go partners in Copenhagen. The sushi counter and every maker here are castings, stand-ins until real humans sign real releases. The shops can be real on day one. The pride already is.

The shortest email TGTG has ever sent a lapsed user, on purpose. CRM pulls the episode from the recipient's nearest active partner, so every lapsed user gets a different, true introduction, and the episode does the persuading instead of the copy. The structure is fixed; the neighbor changes.

05 Deliverable 02c · Social / Paid The Episodes + Carousel One scripted episode and a wall of the rest. The machine behind it lives in 06.

The brief said pick one. The episodes are the pick; the carousel is the same idea standing still, for paid placements that can't move. One concept, not two.

"Meet Your Maker" is not a film. It's a recurring 15-second vertical format: face, name, craft, one dry line, end card. One episode is scripted below to prove the beats; the wall underneath is what the network looks like at scale. No campaign clock, no hero food, no casting hierarchy. Local taste is the casting director.

06 The organic engine The Ask The campaign launches as an open call: introduce yourself.

This campaign doesn't distribute creative to shops. It asks them for something: introduce yourself. 


A public, open call to every partner, all at once. The ask itself is the launch event (the world's largest introduction, and the press writes that headline for us), the brand-shot flagships answer first to set the bar, and the kit below is simply how everyone else answers. 

Partners already post; they have phones, regulars, and pride. The kit doesn't create that behavior, it formats the answer. Most campaigns rent a film crew. This one comes with 180,000 of them.

The 3-shot list

  1. Your face, where you work. Look at the camera.
  2. Your hands, doing the thing you're best at. Making the bread. Cutting the fish. Presenting the food.
  3. The bag, at closing. Handing it to someone if you can.

The prompt card

Say your name, position, and where you work. Say what food you're known for. Then tell us the one thing customers get wrong about the food at the end of the day.

The ladder

  1. Everyone: the kit. Shops film themselves and send it in. TGTG brands and publishes on its own channels.
  2. The best: a crew. Flagships set the bar at launch; after that, top-performing episodes earn the crew visit. These carry the localized paid pushes.
  3. The top 5 to 10: a film. Meet Your Maker: The Films. A proper film about the shop, the people, and the day, built for YouTube and press. Most-watched episodes make the shortlist; editors pick for story. The magic is the subject. The surplus is the twist, never the tragedy.
15 seconds Vertical Real maker, not a spokesperson First name on screen One dry line Shared end card No music swells. Ever.

The TGTG cut · the campaign

Ends on the Meet Your Maker end card. Published on our channels, our logo, our voice, localized city by city so Copenhagen sees Copenhagen's makers and Lyon sees Lyon's. The brand's organic reach grows with every episode, and paid enters last, boosting only what's already proven.

The shop's cut · the thank-you

Same film, ends on their name, hours, and "come by at closing." Theirs to post and promote, free advertising they would never budget for. It's the perk that makes sending footage in a no-brainer, not the distribution plan.


*If we want our branding on this too, we could ask them to tag us and/or add a tasteful watermark or "Made with Too Good To Go"

The loop Every episode is edited twice: identical fifteen seconds, only the last frame changes. The footage is sent to us; we make both cuts. Brand asks → shops send → we publish with our name on it, city by city → paid boosts only proven winners. Best answers earn the crew visit, and the best of those earn the film, so the ladder makes being filmed a status thing among partners. One template, near-zero cost per episode, every episode lands twice (our channels and theirs), and the feed never runs dry. What gets counted: submissions, organic reach on our channels, branded search, and lapsed users coming back. Not impressions. That's the lean-off-paid-UA answer, built into the creative itself.
07 Deliverable 03 · Rationale Why this, and why it works In my voice, under 250 words.

Every surplus campaign makes the same mistake: it markets the food. The food was never the problem.

Surplus feels sad because it feels authorless. A bag of "leftovers" belongs to nobody, so nobody misses it. But no food is actually anonymous. Somebody proofed that dough at four in the morning. Somebody rolled that rice at eleven. Give the food its maker back and "stigmatized leftovers" becomes impossible. You can dismiss surplus. It's much harder to dismiss Kasper.

That's the mechanism: anonymity is the stigma. Fix one, the other goes.

So I didn't write a film. I wrote an ask: introduce yourself. Fifteen seconds: face, name, craft, one dry line, end card. Every shop answers as its own hero, in its own neighborhood. And the footage flows to us. We brand it and run it on our channels, city by city, organically. Their cut comes back to them, free advertising they'd never budget for. Partners aren't doing us a favor. They're getting an ad out of it. That's why it scales. Paid boosts only what's proven.

On tone: the pun does the rebellious work, so everything else plays it straight. Deadpan, warm, zero violins. The makers are proud, mildly annoyed, and right, which is the exact register of every great baker I've ever met.

And the don'ts hold. No codes, no activism, no charity. Just the oldest sales technique, an introduction, aimed at dinner. You show up differently for a person than for a price.

244 / 250 words · Jason Donnelly
08 Before you ask The questions I'd ask me too Hardest first. If I missed one, ask it.

"Will shops actually make these?"

They already do. Shops post constantly; the kit just formats the habit, and the shop's cut hands them an ad about the thing they're proudest of. Shops will compete to be episodes. The end card keeps it ours, and recut rights mean nobody has to police a hundred thousand edits.

"Will we be overwhelmed with video submissions?"

In a perfect world? Yes. That would be a good problem to have. In the world we live in? Probably not. With 180,000 partners, many won't be right for this and many won't do it. But out of the ones that do, I'm hoping for a SOLID 100 we can use: shops that share their insights with us and let us help them introduce their makers. 100 quality videos is 0.0556% of our network. 0.0556%!

"Why does a lapsed user care who made it?"

Because anonymity is the stigma. "Leftovers" is the word for food with no author. Once the author shows up, the dismissal stops working, and a person is harder to swipe past than a price.

"Isn't this just every craft-food ad?"

Craft ads point pride at the 9 a.m. shelf. We point the same pride at closing time, the exact moment the whole category is embarrassed about. Nobody else is standing there, which is what makes it ownable.

"Where's the nudge?"

An introduction creates a small social pull that a discount never does. You show up differently for a person than for a price. That's the behavioral mechanism, and it converts without a single promo code in sight.

"You do know what that phrase means, right?"

Yes. That's the joke, and we never tell it. Played straight, the dark read is a smirk the audience gets to have all by themselves. Acknowledged even once, it becomes a brand being edgy. "Rebellious, not provocative" comes down to who's allowed to wink: here it's them, never us.

Meet Your
Maker.
